transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, I came in because my regular doctor seems concerned that my meal planning has gotten... too tight, I suppose she'd say. But honestly, to me it just feels like keeping things orderly. 

I'm an operations research analyst, so I look at efficiency all day. Actually, right now we're doing this massive workflow optimization for a logistics client, and you wouldn't believe the redundancies they have in their supply chain. Just pallets sitting in warehouses for weeks because nobody bothered to update the routing software since 2015! It’s completely maddening. I spent my entire weekend just staring at their transit logs on my computer, trying to find the bottlenecks. My husband keeps telling me I need to leave work at work, but when you see a system that broken, you just want to fix it, you know? 

Anyway, when I get busy with something like that, I just skip lunch. It’s just easier. I keep breakfast to a simple yogurt, and then I make a very measured dinner when I finally log off. It just ensures the day stays orderly. I don't really see the problem with running my own routine as efficiently as my projects, but my doctor insisted I come talk to you.
Do you ever feel anxious or upset when you can't stick to your planned meals?

Well, yes, I suppose I do get a bit... on edge. It's really about the numbers. Like, if I have to go to a restaurant—which I try to avoid because you just can't track the inputs properly—or if I eat what someone else might call a "normal" dinner, and then I step on the scale the next morning and it's up even a single pound... I just get this sharp panic. It's like I've completely lost control of the system and I have to correct it immediately the next day. 

It reminds me of this time my husband and I went to Italy for our 25th anniversary. Beautiful country, really, but the way they handle their train schedules! We were in Florence, trying to get to Siena, and the board said the train was on time, but then it just... wasn't there. No announcements, no updates on the app. We stood on the platform for an hour and a half. And there was this little espresso stand nearby, and the barista didn't even seem to care that the whole station was backed up. He was just taking his sweet time steaming milk. I mean, the inefficiency of it all just made my skin crawl. We ended up having to rent a car, which threw off our entire itinerary for the next three days. I had a spreadsheet for that trip, you know, color-coded by region, and one delayed train just ruined the whole sequence. 

But anyway, yes, if the scale goes up, I just feel that same kind of panic. I have to fix the numbers right away.
Do you have any other routines or rituals in your daily life that you feel compelled to follow?

Other routines? Hmm. No, I wouldn't say so. I mean, nothing I feel compelled to do, aside from just keeping my meals and my work efficient. I don't have any strange rituals or anything. 

I do like my mornings to run smoothly, of course. Like with the coffee. We actually just bought this new espresso machine because my husband wanted to recreate the coffee we had in Italy—which, as I mentioned, was a disaster of a trip in other ways—but this machine, I'm telling you, the design is completely illogical. The water reservoir is in the back, flush against the wall, so you have to pull the whole heavy unit forward just to refill it. Who designs something like that? It makes zero sense for a standard counter depth. 

It reminds me of the contractor who did our kitchen remodel last year. He put the dishwasher on a right angle to the oven so you literally can't open both doors at the same time. I tried to show him the diagrams I made to optimize the kitchen's workflow triangle, but he just brushed me off. Said it was a plumbing constraint, which I know for a fact it wasn't. It took him three extra months to finish the job, too, and he left drywall dust all over my good Persian rug in the dining room. I had to get it professionally cleaned twice, and even now, if the light hits it just right, I swear I can still see a white film on the burgundy threads. 

But, um... what were we talking about? Oh, right, routines. No, I don't think I have any other rituals. Just keeping the food and the schedule on track.
Do you find yourself getting upset or frustrated when things in your personal or work life don't go according to plan?

Upset? No, I don't really think so. I mean, not truly upset. I get frustrated if people are just being completely illogical, but that's just normal, isn't it? 

Like... well, my husband, Richard, he decided to reorganize the garage last weekend. Bless his heart, he thought he was helping because I've been so busy with that logistics client. But he bought these opaque storage bins. Opaque! How are you supposed to know what's in them without opening every single lid to check? And he didn't even use a proper label maker, he just used a black Sharpie on a piece of masking tape. It looked like a rummage sale. I told him, Richard, this is exactly why we can never find the holiday decorations when we actually need them. 

Which reminds me, the homeowner's association is already sending out emails about the winter light displays, and it's barely autumn. Last year, the Petersons across the street left their giant inflatable snow globe up until March. March! And the motor on that thing just hummed all night long, right outside our master bedroom window. I actually had to buy those expensive noise-canceling curtains just to get some sleep. Which, by the way, were advertised as "100% blackout" but they absolutely let light in around the edges because the rod sits way too far from the drywall. You really have to install a wrap-around rod if you want true darkness, otherwise the streetlamps just bleed right in... 

Wait, I'm sorry, what did you ask me? Frustrated? No, no, I wouldn't say I get upset about plans in general. I just like things to make sense.
Do you have recurring thoughts or ideas that you feel compelled to think about over and over?

Recurring thoughts? Compelled to think about... no, not really. I mean, my mind is always active, obviously, but I wouldn't say I'm forced to think about anything over and over. 

Unless you count work, of course. I've been running the simulations for this new distribution model for a client in Cincinnati, and I swear, I have to go over their dataset a dozen times because their data entry clerks don't seem to understand the fundamental difference between a zero and a null value. It completely skews the predictive algorithms. I had to call their IT director, Kevin, about it on Tuesday. And Kevin—well, he insisted on doing a video call instead of just looking at the spreadsheet I sent. I don't know why everyone wants to do video calls for everything now. You spend the first ten minutes just looking up people's noses while they try to figure out how to unmute themselves. 

Anyway, Kevin had this ceiling fan right above his head that was wobbling so violently I thought it was going to detach and decapitate him right there on the screen. It was one of those cheap brass ones from the nineties with the wicker blades. Honestly, if the mounting bracket is loose, you just need a step stool and a Phillips head screwdriver to tighten the housing, it takes two minutes. My husband Richard tried to install a ceiling fan in our guest room once and didn't balance the blades, so it just ticked all night long. Tick, tick, tick. I finally had to tape a quarter to the top of one of the blades myself to balance the weight distribution because he refused to admit he did it wrong... 

Wait, what were you asking me? Compelled to think about something? Oh. No. No recurring thoughts. Just a lot of general incompetence to deal with, really.
When you say you need to 'correct' your food intake after gaining a pound, what is it about gaining weight that bothers you the most?

What bothers me the most? Well, it's just... if the scale is up even a pound, say, after a normal dinner or if we've gone to a restaurant, I feel this sharp panic. It's like I've completely lost control and I just have to correct it the next day. 

Speaking of restaurants, Richard insisted we go to this new Italian place downtown last Friday, supposedly to make up for that whole espresso machine fiasco. But honestly, the parking situation was a nightmare. They claim they have valet, but it's just one teenager running back and forth to a lot three blocks away. We waited twenty minutes just to drop the car off. And then, when we finally get inside, they seat us right next to the kitchen doors. I mean, right next to them. Every time a waiter came out, I got hit with a blast of hot air and the smell of industrial dish soap. 

I asked the hostess if we could move to a booth by the window—there were clearly three empty ones—but she gave me some nonsense about them being reserved for larger parties. Which is ridiculous, because a four-top is a four-top, regardless of whether two or four people are sitting there. It's basic spatial utilization. I actually drew out a seating chart on a napkin to show Richard how they were completely failing to optimize their floor plan. If they just angled the tables at 45 degrees, they could fit at least two more two-tops in the dining room without violating fire code. 

But anyway... what was the question? Oh, the weight gain. Yes, it's just that feeling of panic, like I've lost control. I just can't stand that feeling.
Is your need to control your food intake and daily routines more about achieving a sense of order or about avoiding a specific negative outcome?

Well, it's definitely about keeping things orderly. I actually only came in today because my primary care doctor got all worked up during my annual physical. He seems terribly concerned that my meal planning has gotten "too tight," which is just an absurd way to phrase it. To me, it just feels like keeping things structured. I have my yogurt for breakfast, I usually just skip lunch if I'm busy with the distribution models, and then I make a very measured, precise dinner so the whole day stays orderly and predictable. 

Speaking of my primary care doctor, Dr. Evans, his waiting room is a complete disaster. They have this massive fish tank right in the middle of the room, which I suppose is meant to be calming, but the filter on it is so loud it sounds like a small outboard motor. And the magazines! They're all from at least two years ago. I picked up a copy of Architectural Digest that was featuring "Trends for 2021." Who wants to read about outdated trends? 

Plus, his receptionist, Brenda, insists on using this incredibly clunky scheduling software. I tried to explain to her that if they just switched to a cloud-based integrated system, she wouldn't have to manually input every single appointment card into the ledger. It's redundant data entry, which is exactly how errors happen. I even offered to send her a spreadsheet template that would automate the reminders, but she just gave me this blank look and handed me a clipboard with a pen attached to a giant plastic flower. A plastic flower! It's impossible to write legibly when you have a fake daisy bouncing around on the end of your pen. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, right, the meal planning. Yes, my doctor thinks it's too strict, but I just like knowing exactly what I'm having and keeping the day orderly. It just makes sense.
Is your concern about gaining weight related to how you think you look or how you feel about your body?

Well, it's... I mean, I know I'm a sixty-three-year-old woman. I'm not delusional. I'm not trying to look like a teenager or anything ridiculous like that. But I do still judge how well I'm handling myself by whether my waist and hips look, you know, contained in my clothes. If things start feeling tight, it just feels sloppy. 

Speaking of sloppy, I had to take my navy blazer to the dry cleaners on Elm Street yesterday because my usual place was closed for renovations. And let me tell you, the woman behind the counter—I think her name tag said 'Doris'—was eating a powdered donut while handling the garments. A powdered donut! The sheer risk of particulate transfer onto dark fabrics is astronomical. I watched her wipe her hands on a tissue and then immediately reach for a silk blouse. I almost said something about establishing a designated break area away from the inventory, but she was already struggling to operate the rotating rack system. 

It's a simple pedal mechanism, really, but she kept stepping on it too hard, so the clothes were just whizzing by. She missed my ticket number three times. If they just calibrated the tension spring on the pedal, it would allow for much more controlled rotation. I actually noticed the track itself looked like it hadn't been lubricated since the Bush administration. A little silicone spray would reduce the friction coefficient by at least forty percent, saving wear and tear on the motor. I told Richard about it when I got home, and he just rolled his eyes and went back to watching his golf tournament. I don't understand how anyone can watch golf on television. It's just hours of whispering and grass. 

Anyway... what did you ask me? Oh, right, my body. Yes, it's just about feeling contained in my clothes. It's a measure of how well I'm managing myself.
Is your desire to control your food intake more about preventing weight gain or about maintaining a sense of structure in your daily life?

Well, as I was saying earlier, it really is about structure. Like I mentioned, Dr. Evans is the one who got all in a twist about it, saying my meal planning is "too tight." But honestly, I just like the orderliness of it. I have my yogurt in the morning, I usually skip lunch because I'm deep into my distribution models, and then dinner is just... very measured. It keeps the whole day predictable. 

But speaking of Dr. Evans, I forgot to mention the absolute state of his parking lot. The lines haven't been repainted in what looks like a decade. People are just guessing where the spaces are! When I pulled in for my appointment, there was a silver sedan parked at such a bizarre angle it was taking up at least a space and a half. It’s a completely inefficient use of square footage. If they just restriped the lot and switched to a herringbone pattern—say, a 60-degree angled parking layout—they could increase their capacity by at least fifteen percent and create a much smoother flow for one-way traffic. 

I actually started sketching out a proposal on the back of a receipt while I was sitting in my car, waiting for Brenda to unlock the front doors. They don't open until exactly 8:00 AM, not a minute before, even if it's raining. Which it was. A light drizzle, but still. I had to sit there watching the wiper blades on that silver sedan—which, by the way, were completely degraded. You could tell by the streaking pattern on the windshield that the rubber had oxidized. 

Anyway... wait, what was the question again? Oh, the food intake. Yes, it's just about keeping the day orderly. Yogurt, skip lunch, measured dinner. It just makes sense to me.
Do you think your life would feel less in control if you didn't plan your meals so strictly?

Well, I suppose so. I mean, if I don't plan it out, things just get... messy. Like if I go to a restaurant with Richard, or just have what people call a "normal" dinner, and the scale is up even a single pound the next morning, I get this sharp panic. It just feels like I've completely lost control of everything, and I immediately have to correct it the next day. 

Speaking of restaurants, Richard dragged me to that new Italian place downtown on Friday. The menu was an absolute nightmare of typography. They used this sweeping cursive font that was practically illegible, especially in the dim lighting they insist on using to create "ambiance." Ambiance shouldn't mean I need a miner's headlamp to read the specials. And the waitstaff! Our server, a young man named Tyler, brought us water but didn't leave the carafe on the table. It's a fundamental failure in service logistics. If you leave the carafe, the customer can self-serve, reducing the server's trips to the table by at least fifty percent and freeing them up to turn over other tables faster. 

I tried to explain the math to Richard, but he was too busy trying to decipher the wine list. They had the wines organized by region instead of varietal, which is just absurd for a casual dining establishment. If you organize by varietal, you streamline the decision-making process for the average consumer. I actually started reorganizing their wine list on the back of a napkin while we waited for our entrees. Tyler came by and looked very confused when I handed it to him with his tip. 

But anyway... what were you asking? Oh, right, the planning. Yes, if the scale goes up even a pound, I just panic. I have to fix it the next day so I don't lose control.
Is your strict meal planning more about preventing weight gain or about maintaining a sense of control in your life?

Well, it's... I suppose it's a bit of both, isn't it? I know my weight has drifted down more than Dr. Evans likes. He showed me the chart last week, and he made this little clicking sound with his tongue that I find entirely unprofessional. But when I look at the graph, I still find myself thinking that a little lower would just be a cleaner, more manageable number. 

Speaking of charts, Dr. Evans's office is still using paper files for at least half their records. It's absolute madness. I saw the receptionist—I think her name was Carol—trying to find a lab report, and she was digging through these manila folders that were practically bursting at the seams. I told her that if they transitioned to a fully integrated cloud-based system, they could reduce retrieval time by eighty percent. And they wouldn't need all those bulky filing cabinets taking up prime real estate in the waiting area. They could put in some actual comfortable chairs instead of those rigid plastic ones that look like they belong in a bus terminal. 

And the magazines! They had a copy of *Better Homes & Gardens* from 2019 on the table. Who wants to read about pre-pandemic patio furniture? I actually started sorting them chronologically while I was waiting. It just makes more sense. If you have the current issues on top, the patient doesn't have to sift through outdated material. It's a simple queuing theory application—last in, first out. 

But anyway... what were we talking about? Oh, the weight. Yes, I just think a slightly lower number would be more manageable. Cleaner, you know?
Is your strict meal planning more about feeling in control of your life or about avoiding weight gain?

Well, it's... I mean, I know I'm an older woman. I'm not trying to look like a twenty-something on the cover of a magazine. But I still judge how well I'm handling myself, how well I'm managing things, by whether my waist and hips look contained in my clothes. It's a metric of success. 

Speaking of clothes, I took a few of my blazers to the dry cleaner on Elm Street last week. The new one, not the one that burned down. And their tagging system is a complete operational failure. They staple these tiny paper tags directly onto the care labels, which not only risks damaging the garment but also slows down the retrieval process at the counter. The clerk—a girl who couldn't have been older than nineteen, chewing gum with her mouth open—had to squint at every single tag to match the numbers to my ticket. 

If they just implemented a barcode scanning system with heat-sealed, temporary adhesive labels, they could process pickups in a fraction of the time. I actually mapped out the workflow on the back of my receipt while I was standing there. It's a basic bottleneck analysis. They're losing at least three minutes per customer during peak hours, which compounds into a massive loss of throughput by the end of the day. I tried to explain this to the manager, but he just stared at me like I was speaking Greek. 

Anyway... what was the question? Oh, right, the clothes. Yes, I just need to feel like my waist and hips are contained. It shows I'm handling myself properly.
Is your strict meal planning something you feel you need to do to feel safe or in control, rather than just to manage your weight?

Safe? I'm not really sure what you mean by safe. I don't think I've ever really looked at it that way, to be honest. I just plan the meals. I haven't really thought about it as a safety mechanism or anything like that. 

Speaking of meal planning, though, I had to go to the grocery store on Tuesday—the big one over on 4th Street—and they have completely overhauled their floor plan. It is a logistical nightmare. They moved the dairy section away from the back perimeter and split it up into two different aisles. Now, I understand the basic retail strategy behind it. They want to force customers to traverse more square footage to increase the probability of impulse buys. But from an operational standpoint, it is an absolute disaster for their restocking efficiency. 

Just think about the cold chain logistics! They had this one young man—he looked utterly exhausted, poor thing—dragging a heavy pallet of milk cartons all the way across the store, dodging shopping carts and endcap displays. If they just kept the high-volume perishables adjacent to the loading docks, they could reduce employee transit time by easily sixty percent. I actually mapped out a more efficient routing matrix on the back of my shopping list and dropped it in the manager's suggestion box. Not that anyone actually reads those. It's probably just a placebo for customer complaints. 

But... I'm sorry, what were we just talking about? Oh, right, feeling safe. Yes, I really couldn't tell you if it's about that. I just haven't noticed it being about safety. I just plan things because I have to.
Do you feel like you would still plan your meals strictly even if you didn't have to worry about your weight?

Well, I... I don't really know. I suppose I haven't ever thought about a scenario where I wouldn't have to worry about my weight. It's just a constant variable in the equation, isn't it? I just plan them because that's what I do. 

Although, speaking of planning, I was trying to organize my kitchen pantry this weekend, and I realized the standardized sizing for canned goods is completely inefficient for modern shelving units. Most residential cabinets are built with a standard depth of twelve inches, but the standard soup can has a diameter of about two and eleven-sixteenths inches. If you try to stack them, you end up with all this dead space in the back. 

I ended up designing a customized, tiered shelving insert out of some spare acrylic I had in the garage. It uses a gravity-fed dispenser model, like they have in commercial vending machines. You put the new cans in the top, and they roll down to the front. First in, first out. It ensures proper inventory rotation and maximizes the cubic volume of the cabinet. I don't know why container stores don't sell something exactly like it. The ones they do sell are either too wide or the pitch angle is wrong, so the cans get stuck halfway down. I actually thought about patenting my design, but the upfront cost for the injection molding prototypes is astronomical right now. 

But... oh dear, I've lost the thread again, haven't I? What were you asking? Oh, about the meal planning without the weight worry. I just... I really couldn't say. I've never been in a position not to worry about it.
Do you think you would be able to stop planning your meals so strictly if you felt more in control of other aspects of your life?

Control of other aspects... I mean, I suppose? I really don't know. I don't think I've ever separated it out like that. Everything just requires a certain level of management, doesn't it? I'm not sure if having a handle on one thing would make me drop the ball on another. 

Actually, speaking of management and dropping the ball, I was at the post office yesterday—the brick one over by the library—and their queuing system is a complete disaster. It is a textbook failure of basic queuing theory. They have four service windows, but they only ever staff one during the lunchtime rush. The arrival rate of customers completely overwhelms their service rate. People were standing there for twenty minutes just to drop off pre-labeled packages. It’s absurd. 

If the postmaster just used a simple Poisson distribution to analyze their daily foot traffic and staggered the staff lunch breaks accordingly, they could virtually eliminate the bottleneck. I was standing there with a parcel for my sister, actually timing the service intervals on my watch. The variance in processing time per customer is huge because the clerk has to keep walking all the way to the back room to retrieve certified mail. If they just batched those retrievals, or reorganized the staging area to be within arm's reach of the terminal... well, I was half tempted to draw a diagram on the back of my envelope and slide it under the glass. 

But... oh, excuse me, I'm rambling again. What did you ask me? About the meals, right? Stopping the planning if I had control elsewhere. I just... I really couldn't say. I don't know if one has anything to do with the other. I just plan them because it needs doing.
Do you feel like planning your meals and daily routines is something you enjoy doing, or is it something you feel like you have to do?

Enjoy doing? Have to do? I... I don't really know. I don't think I've ever stopped to classify it as one or the other. It's just a process that requires execution. I don't know if "enjoyment" is a metric that applies. 

Speaking of processes, I was observing the traffic light sequencing at the intersection of Elm and 5th this morning on my way here. It is wildly inefficient. They have a fixed-time signal control, but the traffic volume is highly directional depending on the time of day. During the morning commute, the eastbound lane backs up for three blocks, while the westbound lane gets a full forty-five seconds of green light for maybe two cars. 

It’s completely nonsensical. If the city just installed a few induction loops or even basic video detection, they could implement an actuated signal system. You could optimize the cycle length and split times dynamically based on real-time demand. I was actually sitting there at the red light, calculating the total aggregate time wasted by all the idling vehicles. The economic loss in terms of fuel consumption and lost productivity must be staggering over a fiscal year. I was thinking about writing a letter to the Department of Transportation, maybe drafting a quick simulation model to prove my point. I have some software on my home computer that could easily handle a basic intersection like that. 

But... wait, I'm sorry, I got distracted again. You were asking about enjoying the meal planning? Or having to do it? Yes, I... I really don't know. It's just a routine. I don't know if I enjoy it or just feel compelled. It's just what happens.
Do you think your need for planning and control is related to feeling overwhelmed by the unpredictability of life?

Unpredictability? I mean, I suppose life is inherently stochastic, but overwhelmed? I don't know if I'd use that word. I just try to mitigate variance where I can. I've never really thought about whether one causes the other. 

Speaking of variance and unpredictability, though, the municipal waste management in my neighborhood has been completely erratic lately. They used to come every Tuesday at exactly 7:15 AM. You could literally set your watch by it. But since they switched to those new automated side-loader trucks last month, their routing is completely unoptimized. They claim the new trucks are more efficient, but I've actually been tracking their pickup times on a spreadsheet, and the standard deviation is nearly four hours! 

Sometimes they come at 6 AM, sometimes not until 2 PM. It completely disrupts the street parking dynamic because everyone leaves their bins out all day, blocking the curbs. If the sanitation department just used a basic traveling salesperson algorithm and factored in the varying density of the recycling bins versus the solid waste on different blocks, they could tighten up their route times significantly. I even thought about calling the city planner's office to offer a pro bono consultation. It's just sloppy logistics, and it drives me absolutely up the wall when a system is running that far below its optimal capacity. 

But... oh, goodness, I'm doing it again. I am so sorry. You were asking about life being unpredictable, and if that's why I plan things so much? I really couldn't tell you. I just... I don't really know if they're connected like that. I just like things to be orderly.
Do you feel like your need to plan meals and control your weight is related to any recurring, intrusive thoughts or compulsions you might have?

Intrusive thoughts? Compulsions? I... I'm not really sure what you mean by that. I mean, I think about the meals, obviously, but I don't know if I'd call it intrusive. It's just part of the schedule. I don't really know if it's a compulsion or just... just what I do. 

Speaking of schedules, I was at the grocery store yesterday—the one on 4th Street, with the terrible parking lot—and their inventory management system is completely broken. I was looking for a specific brand of low-sodium broth, and the shelf was completely empty, but the tag said they had twelve units in stock. It's a classic case of phantom inventory. They're probably using a periodic review system instead of a continuous review system, which is just asking for stockouts on high-velocity items. 

And the way they restock is completely haphazard. They had a pallet of paper towels sitting right in the middle of the aisle during peak shopping hours. If they just implemented a simple just-in-time inventory model and scheduled their deliveries for off-peak hours, they could improve their floor space utilization by at least thirty percent. I was actually standing there, looking at the empty shelf, thinking about how easy it would be to write a script that cross-references their point-of-sale data with their warehouse shipments to flag those discrepancies automatically. I almost asked to speak to the store manager, just to point out how much revenue they're losing to stockouts. 

But... oh, I'm sorry. I lost my train of thought again. You were asking about... compulsions? And the meal planning? Yeah, I really don't know. I don't think I have anything like that. I just plan things out.
Do you feel like planning your meals is something you do to relieve anxiety or distress, rather than just to maintain order?

Anxiety? Distress? I mean, I suppose everyone feels anxious sometimes, but I don't know if the meal planning is meant to relieve it. I really couldn't say. It's just... it's just the plan. 

Speaking of plans, though, I was looking at the architectural blueprints for the new library expansion they're building downtown. They posted them on the city council website for public comment, and I have to say, the spatial flow is completely illogical. They have the main circulation desk tucked away in this corner that creates a massive bottleneck right at the entrance, especially if you factor in the foot traffic from the children's section. 

It’s like they didn't run a single queuing theory model before they finalized the floor plan. If they just moved the self-checkout kiosks ten feet to the left and angled the main desk, they could increase throughput by at least forty percent during peak hours. I actually spent about three hours last night sketching out an alternative layout. I was thinking of taking it down to the next zoning board meeting. It just bothers me so much when a public space is designed with zero consideration for operational efficiency. It's going to be a nightmare when they open. 

But... wait, what were we talking about? Anxiety? And the meals? Right, I... I don't know. I don't think I do it to relieve distress. I just... I just like knowing what the numbers are.
Do you feel like your strict meal planning and daily routines are a way for you to exert control over your life, or is it more about achieving a sense of order and efficiency?

Control over my life? Or just order? I... I'm not really sure how to distinguish the two, to be honest. I don't know if I'm trying to control my whole life. I haven't really analyzed it that way. It's just about keeping things running efficiently, I suppose. 

Speaking of efficiency, though, the traffic light synchronization on Elm Street is an absolute disaster right now. I was driving down there yesterday afternoon, and I hit every single red light for two miles. It’s a classic failure in network flow optimization. They clearly haven't updated their signal timing plans to account for the new residential development on the west side. If they just implemented a dynamic phasing system that responds to real-time traffic volume instead of relying on fixed-time cycles, they could reduce idle times by at least twenty percent. 

I actually sat at the intersection of Elm and 5th for three cycles, just counting the cars and calculating the delay per vehicle. It’s so frustrating because it’s such a simple linear programming problem to solve. I was half-tempted to pull over, draft a quick proposal, and email it to the Department of Transportation right from my phone. It just physically pains me to see a system operating with that much unnecessary friction, wasting everyone's fuel and time. 

But... oh dear, I've gone off track again, haven't I? I am so sorry, my mind just latches onto these things. You were asking if my meals are about control or order? Honestly, I don't really know. I just haven't thought about it in those terms. I just like my routine to be exactly what it is.
